chapters.title: Chapter 5: Evaluating Startups and Building Your Portfolio

lessons.title: Evaluating a Startup: Founders, Market, Product and Traction

children.text: A founder gets 20 minutes to pitch. You get a few evenings to decide whether to hand over ₹10 lakh. Most first-time angels decide on gut feel: the founder was impressive, the deck was slick, a friend is investing. That is how people end up backing charismatic founders in markets too small to matter, or products nobody uses twice. This lesson gives you a structured way to evaluate any early-stage startup across four pillars, founders, market, product and traction, with the specific evidence, numbers and red flags to look for in each.

body.text: At seed stage you are not valuing a business. You are judging whether a team can find a big enough market before the money runs out. Score founders, market, product and traction separately, so one shiny strength cannot hide a fatal weakness.

children.text: Pillar 1: Founders

markDefs.definition: When a founder's experience, relationships or insight give them an unusual advantage in solving the specific problem they have chosen.

children.text: At the earliest stage, the team is most of what you are buying, because the product and strategy will change. Look for
founder-market fit

, speed of execution and, above all, integrity. And judge evidence, not stereotypes. Great Indian founders do not fit one template: Falguni Nayar spent 18 years with Kotak Mahindra Capital, rising to managing director, before founding Nykaa in April 2012, when she was around 50.

body.caption: What to assess in a founding team

cells: Years in the industry, direct experience of the pain, a non-obvious view of the market
Chose the idea from a trend report; cannot explain why customers behave as they do
Shipped a product and signed customers with very little money
Months of "building" with nothing live; long list of plans, short list of results
Numbers that match documents; openly shares bad news
Inflated metrics, vague answers on past ventures, pressure to decide fast
Complementary skills, such as one founder on product and technology, one on sales
Critical skills fully outsourced to an agency; key hires always "coming soon"
Full-time founders, their own money in, founder shares that vest over time
Founders still in day jobs; no vesting; large salaries from the round
Changes course when evidence says so; seeks out criticism
Treats every question as an attack

body.title: Eight questions to ask founders, and how to check the answers

children.text: Why are you the right people to solve this, and what do you know that others do not?
What have you tried that failed, and what did you change?
How much of your own money and time is in the company?
How do the founders split decisions, and what happens if you disagree?
Which three customers can I speak to, including one who stopped using you?
What exactly will this round's money achieve, and by when?
What would make you shut the company down?
Can I see your bank statements, GST returns and cap table?

Then check independently. Speak to former colleagues and earlier investors the founder did not suggest, call customers yourself, and match claimed revenue against GST filings and MCA records. Reference calls you arrange yourself are worth far more than the ones the founder sets up.
Pillar 2: Market

markDefs.definition: Total Addressable Market: the total annual revenue available if every possible customer bought the product.
Serviceable Addressable Market: the part of the TAM the company can realistically reach with its product, geography and sales model.
Serviceable Obtainable Market: the share of the SAM the company can plausibly win in the next few years.

children.text: The power law means a startup must be able to become very large. Market size is usually described as
TAM
SAM
and
SOM
. Ignore any slide that says "a $50 billion market, we only need 1%". Build the number yourself from the bottom up: count the real customers and multiply by what each will actually pay.

body.latex: \text{Bottom-up TAM} = \text{Number of target customers} \times \text{Annual revenue per customer}
body.caption: Then narrow it: SAM is the part the company can actually reach, and SOM is the part it can plausibly win in the next few years.
LabLink, a software startup for diagnostic labs (all assumptions illustrative)

cells: 30% are urban labs ready to adopt software

body.text: ₹5.4 crore of revenue in five years may be a fine small business, but in Chapter 3 you saw that a 100x angel return can require a ₹2,500 crore exit. Unless LabLink can raise prices, sell more products to each lab or expand into hospitals and other countries, the market is too small for angel-style returns, however good the founders are.

body.title: Size the market
body.prompt: An edtech startup sells a school management app. It estimates 25,000 private schools as target customers, each paying ₹50,000 a year. What is its bottom-up TAM, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: 25,000 × ₹50,000 = ₹1,25,00,00,000, or ₹125 crore. Now ask the next questions: how many of those schools can the company actually reach, how many already use a competitor, and could it sell additional products to push revenue per school higher?

children.text: Pillar 3: Product
Use the product yourself, and watch real customers use it if you can. Four questions matter most:
How painful is the problem?
Customers pay quickly to remove real pain; they postpone "nice to have" purchases.
Why is it better?
It should be clearly better, cheaper or faster than the current alternative, which is often Excel, WhatsApp or a manual process.
Why now?
A change such as UPI adoption, a new regulation or cheaper AI makes this possible today when it was not five years ago.
What stops copying?
Network effects, proprietary data, deep integration into customers' workflows or a brand are harder to copy than features.

columns.label: Painkiller product
points: Solves a problem customers complain about without prompting
Customers pay even when budgets are tight
Usage stays high after the novelty wears off
Sales conversations focus on price and timing, not on persuading

columns.label: Vitamin product
points: Makes something slightly nicer or more convenient
First to be cut when money is short
Usage fades after a few weeks
Growth depends on discounts and marketing spend

children.text: Pillar 4: Traction and Unit Economics

markDefs.definition: Customer Acquisition Cost: total sales and marketing spend divided by the number of new customers acquired in that period.
Lifetime Value: the gross profit a customer generates over the whole time they stay with the company.
A chart tracking what percentage of customers who started in the same month are still active in later months.

children.text: Revenue growth gets the attention, but the quality of that growth matters more. The core numbers are
CAC
LTV
and
retention cohorts
. Calculate LTV on gross profit, not revenue, or you will overstate it.

body.latex: \text{LTV} = \text{Gross profit per order} \times \text{Orders per year} \times \text{Years retained} \qquad \text{Health check} = \frac{\text{LTV}}{\text{CAC}}
body.caption: A common rule of thumb is an LTV to CAC ratio of at least 3, with CAC recovered within roughly 12 months.
Unit economics of an illustrative D2C ethnic-wear brand

body.title: Check the SaaS ratio
body.prompt: A SaaS startup charges ₹2,000 per month with an 80% gross margin. The average customer stays 30 months, and CAC is ₹12,000. What is its LTV to CAC ratio?
body.explanation: Gross profit per month = ₹2,000 × 80% = ₹1,600. LTV = ₹1,600 × 30 = ₹48,000. LTV ÷ CAC = ₹48,000 ÷ ₹12,000 = 4x, above the common 3x benchmark. CAC payback is ₹12,000 ÷ ₹1,600 = 7.5 months.

body.title: Retention cohorts: leaky bucket vs flattening curve (% of customers still active, illustrative)

body.text: A retention curve that flattens, like Startup B's, is one of the strongest signs of product-market fit: a stable group of customers keeps coming back without being chased. A curve that keeps sliding towards zero means growth is only refilling a leaking bucket, and more marketing spend will not fix it.

body.caption: Scoring LabLink out of 5 on each pillar (weights and scores illustrative)

body.label: The knockout rule
body.value: Any serious doubt about integrity ends the evaluation
body.context: Weighted scores help compare deals, but they must not average away a fatal flaw. Also treat a score of 2 or less on market as a reason to pass unless the founders have a credible expansion path.

body.title: The strongest signal
body.question: Which of these is the strongest evidence of product-market fit for an early-stage consumer app?
options: 2 lakh downloads in the first month after a paid influencer campaign
A retention cohort that levels off at around 40% of users still active after six months
A founder with a degree from a top engineering college
A pitch deck citing a $20 billion market
body.explanation: Downloads can be bought, credentials say nothing about demand, and top-down market sizes are easy to inflate. A retention curve that flattens shows a lasting group of users who keep coming back on their own, which is what product-market fit looks like in the data.

body.title: Pallavi evaluates a chikankari marketplace
body.scenario:
Pallavi, an angel in Delhi, is evaluating a Lucknow-based B2B marketplace connecting chikankari artisans with boutiques across India.
Founders: one spent six years as a category manager at a large fashion e-commerce company; the other grew up in an artisan family and manages supply.
Traction: ₹40 lakh of monthly orders, growing 15% a month; the company earns a 12% commission; 55% of boutiques reorder within 90 days.
Economics: acquiring a boutique costs ₹6,000; an active boutique orders about ₹20,000 a month.
The round: ₹2 crore at a ₹16 crore post-money valuation.
body.prompt: Evaluate the startup on the four pillars. What looks strong, what worries you, and what would you check before investing?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Founders: strong founder-market fit, combining e-commerce category experience with deep access to artisans. Check references with former colleagues, and confirm both are full-time with vesting shares.
2. Market: chikankari alone may be a niche. Pallavi should build a bottom-up estimate of boutiques that could buy, and test the founders' plan to add other crafts such as Banarasi, Kalamkari or Phulkari, which could make the market large enough.
3. Product: a B2B marketplace solves a real pain on both sides, finding reliable supply and reaching buyers. Ask what stops boutiques from dealing directly with artisans after the first order, since that leakage can destroy marketplaces.
4. Traction and unit economics: commission per active boutique is ₹20,000 × 12% = ₹2,400 a month, so the ₹6,000 acquisition cost is recovered in about 2.5 months on revenue, which looks healthy, although logistics, returns and payment costs must be subtracted to get true gross profit. A 55% reorder rate within 90 days is encouraging; she should ask for full monthly cohorts.
5. Checks before investing: GST filings against claimed order volume, boutique references including ones that stopped ordering, gross margin after logistics and returns, and working capital needs if the company pays artisans before boutiques pay it.

body.title: The rule of thumb
body.textWithBlank: A commonly used benchmark is that a startup's LTV should be at least ___ times its CAC.
body.explanation: An LTV to CAC ratio of 3x or more suggests each customer generates enough gross profit to justify what it cost to acquire them. It is a rule of thumb, not a law, and depends on how long it takes to recover the CAC.

cards.definition: When founders' experience or insight gives them an unusual advantage in solving their chosen problem.
Total Addressable Market: total annual revenue if every possible customer bought the product.
Serviceable Addressable Market: the part of TAM the company can realistically reach.
Serviceable Obtainable Market: the share of SAM the company can plausibly win in a few years.
Customer Acquisition Cost: sales and marketing spend divided by new customers acquired.
Lifetime Value: gross profit a customer generates over their entire relationship with the company.
How many months of gross profit it takes to recover the cost of acquiring a customer.
A chart of what share of customers from the same starting month are still active over time.

points: Evaluate founders, market, product and traction separately, so one strength cannot hide a fatal weakness.
Founders matter most at seed: look for founder-market fit, execution speed, commitment and integrity, and verify through references you arrange yourself.
Build market size bottom-up, customers × annual revenue per customer, and check it can support a very large company.
Prefer painkiller products that are clearly better than the current alternative, with a reason they are possible now and hard to copy.
Judge traction by quality: LTV on gross profit, an LTV to CAC ratio of around 3x or more, fast CAC payback and retention curves that flatten.
Use a weighted scorecard to compare deals, but let any integrity concern end the evaluation outright.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Benchmarks such as the 3x LTV to CAC ratio are rules of thumb that vary by sector and stage. LabLink, the D2C brand, the chikankari marketplace, Pallavi and all figures are illustrative. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before investing.
